record.paper_title: Realistic shell-model calculations: current status and open problems
record.original_question: For low-momentum shell-model effective interactions derived from phase-shift equivalent nucleon-nucleon potentials, how sensitive are the resulting shell-model observables to moderate variations of the cutoff momentum Λ, and how should that cutoff dependence be characterized or controlled?

evidence.quote: We have found [25], however, that the shell-model results do not change significantly for moderate variations of the cutoff around this value.
Further study is certainly needed to better clarify the effect of cutoff variations on shell-model effective interactions.

artifact.self_contained_problem:
Consider the construction of low-momentum nucleon–nucleon effective interactions $V_{\text{low-}k}$ obtained by integrating out momentum components above a cutoff $\Lambda$ from a realistic, phase-shift equivalent nucleon–nucleon potential $V_{NN}$, in such a way that the half-on-shell $T$-matrix and deuteron pole are preserved for relative momenta $p,p' < \Lambda$. Use $V_{\text{low-}k}(\Lambda)$ as the input for deriving a shell-model effective interaction $H_{\text{eff}}$ in a chosen valence model space (for example via the $\hat{Q}$-box folded-diagram expansion), and compute resulting shell-model observables $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda)$ such as ground-state binding energies, low-lying excitation spectra, and electromagnetic transition strengths in finite nuclei.

Problem: Quantitatively characterize the dependence of $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda)$ on the cutoff $\Lambda$ for moderate variations of $\Lambda$ around the standard value $\Lambda \approx 2~\mathrm{fm}^{-1}$. Specifically:

1. Establish under what conditions on $V_{NN}$, on the regulator (sharp vs. smooth), and on the truncation of the folded-diagram series the residual $\Lambda$-dependence of $\mathcal{O}(\Lambda)$ is small.
2. Identify the leading sources of the residual cutoff dependence (omitted induced many-body forces, truncation of the $\hat{Q}$-box, model-space truncation), and quantify their respective contributions.
3. Propose a systematic procedure—e.g., inclusion of induced three-nucleon forces, similarity renormalization group consistency, or a cutoff-running equation for $H_{\text{eff}}$—that controls and ideally eliminates the cutoff dependence of shell-model observables to a prescribed accuracy.
artifact.status_search_result: Available literature reports that shell-model results are empirically only weakly sensitive to moderate variations of the $V_{\text{low-}k}$ cutoff around $\Lambda \approx 2~\mathrm{fm}^{-1}$, especially for sharp or sufficiently narrow smooth regulators with $\Lambda > 1.6~\mathrm{fm}^{-1}$. However, a complete quantitative characterization and a systematic procedure to control the residual cutoff dependence—particularly through consistent inclusion of induced many-body forces—remains an active research problem, suggesting the question is partially understood but not fully resolved.

status_evidence.title: Model-independent low momentum nucleon interaction from phase shift equivalence
status_evidence.snippet: V_low-k interactions from various NN potential models are nearly identical when a cutoff Λ ≈ 2 fm⁻¹ or smaller is employed.
status_evidence.claim: Cutoff insensitivity of V_low-k around Λ≈2 fm⁻¹ is established for the bare interaction.

status_evidence.title: Shell-model calculations and realistic effective interactions
status_evidence.snippet: V_low-k is suitable for direct use as a shell-model effective interaction; cutoff dependence of shell-model results requires further study.
status_evidence.claim: Shell-model use of V_low-k is established but residual cutoff dependence is still under investigation.

status_evidence.title: Low-momentum nucleon-nucleon interaction and shell-model calculations
status_evidence.snippet: Cutoff dependence is very weak for sharp or sufficiently narrow smooth regulators with cutoffs Λ>1.6 fm⁻¹.
status_evidence.claim: Empirical weak cutoff dependence supports partial resolution but not a complete theoretical control.
